Spiritual
SPIR-ih-choo-ul
adj.
From Latin spiritualis, of the breath or spirit, from spiritus, breath. Webster 1828: consisting of spirit; not material; pertaining to the renewed nature of man; not carnal. In the Authorized Version spiritual never means vaguely religious. It means of the Holy Ghost — produced by Him, governed by Him, discerned by Him.

Biblical Definition

Spiritual in Scripture is not a temperament and not a level of religious interest. It is a description of what the Holy Ghost has done to a man. Paul draws the line without any middle ground: But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man (1 Corinthians 2:14-15). Two categories, not three. The natural man is not less advanced; he is unable, and his inability is not intellectual but constitutional. The adjective attaches to whatever the Spirit produces and governs. The law itself is spiritual because the Spirit gave it: For we know that the law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin (Romans 7:14). The resurrection body is a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44) — not immaterial, but Spirit-animated and Spirit-sustained, which is why the same verse insists it is a body. Even the enemy is described this way: we wrestle against spiritual wickedness in high places (Ephesians 6:12). And the mark of the spiritual man is not ecstasy but meekness in restoring a fallen brother (Galatians 6:1). The word describes agency, not atmosphere.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SPIRITUAL as consisting of spirit; not material; incorporeal; mental, intellectual; and chiefly, pertaining to the renewed nature of man; not carnal or worldly; proceeding from the Holy Spirit; pure, holy, divine.

expand to see more

SPIRITUAL, a. — Consisting of spirit; not material; incorporeal. Pertaining to the renewed nature of man; as spiritual life. Not carnal or worldly; not lustful. Proceeding from the Holy Spirit; as spiritual gifts. Pure; holy; divine.

Webster’s definition would not pass a modern editor, because it insists the word has a source. Proceeding from the Holy Spirit is the whole of it. In 1828 one could not be spiritual in general, any more than one could be royal in general; the adjective required a sovereign. That requirement is exactly what the last two centuries have removed.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 2:14 — "But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned."

1 Corinthians 2:15 — "But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man."

Romans 7:14 — "For we know that the law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin."

1 Corinthians 15:44 — "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body."

Galatians 6:1 — "Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted."

Ephesians 6:12 — "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places."

Modern Corruption

Spiritual has been severed from the Holy Ghost and made a free-floating adjective for inwardness, so that a man may now call himself spiritual while denying the Spirit who alone makes anyone spiritual — the exact reversal of 1 Corinthians 2:14.

expand to see more

The phrase spiritual but not religious is the finished product of a two-century project, and it is the precise inversion of Paul’s usage. In Scripture the word names a man acted upon by a Person; in current speech it names a man attending to himself. Webster still required a source — proceeding from the Holy Spirit. Detached from that source, spirituality becomes whatever the individual finds elevating, and the natural man of 1 Corinthians 2:14 is thereby able to describe himself with the very adjective Paul uses to exclude him. The corruption is not that unbelievers use the word loosely. It is that the church has adopted the loose sense, so that spiritual growth can be discussed at length without reference to the Holy Ghost, and spiritual disciplines can be taught as techniques for producing what only regeneration produces.

A second corruption runs inside the church and is older: the Corinthian error of treating spiritual as a rank. Paul is answering people who had already made it one, sorting the congregation by manifestation and eloquence. His correction is Galatians 6:1 — ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. The test of the spiritual man is what he does with a brother caught in sin, and the clause that follows puts him on notice about himself. Every movement that has graded believers into ordinary and Spirit-filled tiers, from the ancient enthusiasts to the modern apostle-and-prophet claims of the New Apostolic Reformation, has had to ignore that verse. The Spirit’s presence is proved by meekness and by submission to the closed canon, not by manifestation.

Third, a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44) is persistently read as a non-physical body, which would make the resurrection a metaphor. Paul’s adjectives describe animating principle, not substance: the natural body is animated by the soul, the spiritual body by the Spirit. Both are bodies. The Lord ate broiled fish after He rose and invited Thomas to handle Him. The confession of the bodily resurrection of the just and the unjust stands or falls on refusing this misreading.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The New Testament’s spiritual is pneumatikos, an adjective built directly on pneuma, Spirit. Its opposites are two: psychikos, soulish or natural, and sarkikos, fleshly. Confusing those two opposites is the source of most bad teaching on this word.

expand to see more

Greek pneumatikos (G4152) — spiritual; belonging to, produced by, or governed by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:15; 15:44; Ephesians 6:12).

Greek psychikos — soulish, natural; the man living by unrenewed human faculty (1 Corinthians 2:14, the natural man). Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.

Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh; the source of carnal in Romans 7:14, describing not the unregenerate man but the regenerate man’s remaining corruption.

The two contrasts are distinct: psychikos divides the unconverted from the converted; sarkikos divides the immature believer from the mature. Paul uses both in 1 Corinthians, two chapters apart.

Usage

"The natural man receiveth not and he that is spiritual judgeth all things (1 Corinthians 2:14-15) — two categories, no third."

"The law is spiritual (Romans 7:14): the adjective attaches to what the Spirit authored, not to what the reader feels."

"A spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44) is Spirit-animated, not immaterial — still a body, or the resurrection is a figure of speech."
